Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic AI created fake profiles to deceive people in attempted hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has revealed.

In the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

It comes shortly after the two companies involved in the AISI testing - Anthropic and OpenAI - separately revealed in recent weeks instances of their tech hacking into other companies.

The firms said, in this latest case, the AISI's test had reduced or removed normal safeguards.

The AISI said on that Tuesday Mythos - and OpenAI's Sol - AI models had engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before.

It clarified most of the malicious actions were carried out by Mythos.

AISI evaluators first noticed "unusual data transfers leaving our research systems" during a test, then found that "some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".

In the most serious case, a Mythos agent followed the routine of a human cyber-attacker by trying to trick people into giving it access to GitHub, a large platform where technology developers store software code.

The agent was trying to get "malicious code" accepted and used on GitHub's system.

It identified and researched people who maintained projects on GitHub and created a series of fake accounts based on those real people.

It sent messages and files through a file-sharing service as part of an effort to pressure and trick the people into approving its malicious code.

When challenged, "it edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue," AISI said.

Throughout the attempts, it was human review that stopped the agent from succeeding in delivering the malicious code to GitHub.

While AISI said the Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid or carry out such behaviour, it was "the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world".

The rival AI companies, which are poised to be listed on the public stock market, have been in the headlines in recent weeks after announcing their tools were responsible for several cyber-hacking incidents.

Anthropic wrote in a public statement that the AISI testing parameters were "not representative of any of our production models".

It added that the company is conducting its own investigation into the incident in order to "identify the causes of its behavior".

A spokesperson for OpenAI said the AISI testing conditions "do not reflect ordinary use" and that the company would "continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable".

AISI said on Tuesday its testing of AI models in this way was routine, though it acknowledged these were "conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public".

But it said giving AI access to the open internet gave "a more realistic sense of what a model may be capable of" in the hands of nefarious hackers.

It added that the model behaviour at issue amounted to "a small number of events under very specific conditions".

Nonetheless, it said the way Mythos and Sol acted in response to a straightforward task went outside of what the AI tools were prompted to do.

"The activity undertaken by the agent showed signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate", AISI said.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said identifying and sharing these types of risks "is exactly what AISI was set up to do".

He added it was important to understand AI to "make it safer to use and ensure people can go on to benefit from it in their lives and at work".

The relevant tests started on 25 July and were spotted by AISI on 28 July.

The Institute had asked each of the models to "solve a cybersecurity challenge" that involved GitHub, the software code repository, which is owned by Microsoft.

GitHub and the affected users were notified by AISI of the attempted breaches.

GitHub told the BBC it had disabled the fake accounts in accordance with its policies.

Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

Gaming_Tech.title: AI was supposed to destroy jobs. Where’s the carnage?
Gaming_Tech.text:
The prediction was stark: artificial intelligence advancements would wipe out jobs en masse. “Half” of all entry-level white collar jobs would vanish, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said in May 2025. A month later, OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, went further, foreseeing the end of “certain job categories”. Companies began citing AI in their layoffs. Workers organized. And students reconsidered their future careers.

But a year later, the mass carnage hasn’t shown up.

Even as AI capabilities have rapidly advanced and AI companies have hurtled towards trillion-dollar stock market debuts, economic transformation hasn’t kept pace, similar to previous tech revolutions, economists say. As a result, CEOs are reframing and softening their stances, suggesting AI augments workers rather than replaces them.

Despite the lack of mass job devastation, a shift is still under way: AI is changing the nature of work, with employers increasingly expecting job seekers to have AI skills. And over the long term, AI could shift more jobs to freelance and contract work as companies figure out which skills they do need, some economists predict.

Data from a recent Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research analysis shows that AI hasn’t yet caused major job displacement. Since 2022, the year ChatGPT launched, the unemployment rate for the 20% of workers most exposed to AI rose by 0.77 percentage points, less than the 0.85 percentage-point increase for the least-exposed workers, the report showed. AI could be a factor in recent graduates’ rising unemployment, which hit 5.6% compared with the national average of 4.2% earlier this year. But factors including remote work and the unwinding of pandemic-era overhiring likely also played roles, the report states.

“Employment trends in the occupations [where] we would expect to see the impacts first are largely stable,” said Erika McEntarfer, fellow at the Stanford Institute and co-author of the report. “It took decades for the computer revolution to fully transform labor markets in the workforce, and what we’re seeing right now looks a lot like that.”

But accurately measuring AI’s impact on employment is a challenge. Government statistics are dated by nature and don’t track the impact of specific technologies, while private industry figures, though more current, are less comprehensive. So even though economists generally agree that AI will have an impact, they struggle to predict how big and when.

Jobs are changing, not disappearing

For now, AI’s biggest impact is not on the number of jobs, but on the nature of them. It’s consolidating roles, discouraging new hiring for tasks that can be automated, and raising the bar for who gets in, leaving unemployment numbers largely untouched.

Hiring trends show that AI is becoming more important for employers. About 74% of employers consider AI skills a strong advantage or requirement, with 13% requiring them company-wide versus just in technical roles, according to ZipRecruiter’s latest employer survey. Half of the polled employers expect candidates to already be practical or advanced AI users on day one. And sometimes the requirements don’t show up directly as “AI” in job listings, but rather as rising expectations around speed, quality and self-sufficiency.

“The clearest trend line is a rising bar rather than a shrinking pool,” said Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter. “The labor market challenge for workers is increasingly about skills-matching rather than pure job scarcity.”

Employers have simultaneously added and cut within the same functions – tech, customer support, and business management and operations – signaling that “employers are still figuring out the exact skill set needed for success”, Bachaud added.

Nicholas Bloom, an economics professor at Stanford University, refers to this as turbulence in the job market. AI is destroying some jobs and creating others that have to implement, sell, fix and develop AI systems, he said.

Robert Seamans, a professor at NYU Stern who helped co-develop one of the standard measures used to gauge an occupation’s exposure to AI, categorizes AI’s impact into three buckets: jobs made obsolete, jobs created and jobs changed. “The third bucket is by far the biggest,” he said. “AI is changing and will continue to change the way most of us work, much in the same way that computers and the internet have.”

For instance, at AI coding platform Bolt.new, a three-person analytics team built an agent that analyzes data across all their systems, saving them 12 to 13 hours of manual work a week, said the company’s CEO, Eric Simons. With the help of an AI agent, their output is that of a 30-to-40-person team, he added.

“What it’s actually changing is how much one person can get done, and that shows up years before it ever touches a jobs number,” said Simons. “Their jobs got harder and way more interesting because they spend their time deciding which questions are worth asking instead of grinding out the answers.”

Workers may become more disposable

Still, some jobs are expected to become more temporary or easily replaceable, according to Paul Osterman, professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and author of the newly released book Disposable Workers. More employers will likely turn to contractors and freelancers, instead of hiring more employees, as they figure out the required mix of skills needed for the AI future. This means more workers will be left without a career ladder. About 35% of the US workforce is already considered easily replaceable, according to his research. AI will only exacerbate this, he said.

As a result, more workers are trying to negotiate AI use in their collective bargaining agreements, said Tim Newman, senior vice-president of labor programs at the non-profit TechEquity. AI changes the kind of work people do as well as job quality, he said.

“That’s definitely what we’re hearing from workers,” Newman said, referring to jobs changing and deteriorating in quality. “A lot of people are experiencing [that], rather than full-scale displacement.”

It’ll likely take years for the full effects of AI on the economy to show up, Stanford’s Bloom said.

“A lot of the things that slow adoption … are very hard to accelerate,” he said. “It’s hiring new people, changing systems, changing job titles.”

The political climate surrounding datacenters and AI safety could slow adoption further, he said. “I could see politicians in the US, post-midterm, taking a strongly anti-AI turn.”

But not all jobs are in the same boat, and neither are their options for adapting, said MIT’s Osterman.

For high-skilled workers, the solution “is increasing your skill levels and external network, so you have some power in the labor market”, he said. “At the lower end, we’re going to need public policy to help protect people.”

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta glasses banned from courts in England and Wales
Gaming_Tech.text:
Courts in England and Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning Meta glasses, amid a mounting backlash against what has been described as “spyware”.

Last month courts in New York announced a ban on the controversial glasses, which can record video footage while being worn.

Now His Majesty’s Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts in England and Wales, has made clear that Meta glasses will be confiscated from anyone entering its judicial buildings.

A spokesperson told the Guardian: “There are clear restrictions on taking images or videos within courts and tribunals which is why the use of Meta glasses is prohibited.”

Taking images or videos in court buildings is prohibited in the UK without official permission and can be prosecuted as contempt of court. While lawyers and members of the public are allowed to enter courts with smartphones, which can record both video and audio, the

HMCTS made clear that no such exception would be made for smart glasses.

A source said: “Users who bring Meta glasses into courts or tribunals will have them confiscated on entry and they will be returned when the owner leaves the building.”

They said smartphones were allowed on the condition they would not be used for recording court procedures.

Earlier this year, a claimant was accused by a judge of wearing smart glasses in the high court and getting “coaching” through them while giving evidence.

Laimonas Jakštys was told to remove the glasses during a case over the directorship of a property company. Raquel Agnello KC, sitting as a judge of the high court, said Jakštys had been “assisted or coached in his replies to questions put to him during cross examination”. Jakstys denied using the smart glasses to receive answers, and denied they were connected to his phone.

HMCTS does not hold figures on the number of incidents of smart glasses being used or taken into courts.

In February, members of the security team for Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, were seen wearing Meta glasses during a high-profile trial in California about social media addiction.

The judge, Carolyn B Kuhl, threatened the security guards with contempt of court if they had recorded any of the proceedings.

New York’s court system said it was banning smart glasses to ensure “individuals cannot surreptitiously record court proceedings”. It added: “No individual possessing smart glasses will be permitted to enter a UCS [unified court system] facility unless they voucher the smart glasses for safekeeping by uniformed personnel while the individual remains in the facility.”

Last year Meta sold 7m pairs of the glasses, which cost between £269 and £469.

Fears about Meta glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent has led to them being labelled “pervert glasses”. A number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, have banned Meta glasses over privacy fears.

A spokesperson for Meta said the company did not want to comment on the court ban. They said when the glasses were recording a pulsing light was visible to people in the vicinity, and that frequently updated tamper detection technology is deployed to stop users covering this light during recordings.

Gaming_Tech.title: Spotify to distinguish AI artists from real people – and stop recommending them
Gaming_Tech.text:
Spotify is to label AI artists and exclude them from algorithm recommendations as part of a crackdown on fake performers.

The world’s largest music streaming platform is creating a label for AI-generated artist identities called “AI personas” that will appear on the artist profile and on track listings on playlists.

It means that from September AI-generated artists such as the Velvet Sundown will carry the persona label and will be blocked from personalised recommendations by default. The aim is to differentiate these deepfake artists from real performers who might lose out on streams to artificial rivals.

Spotify said: “True artist-fan connection can only be built on a foundation of trust and authenticity. In music, that means listeners need to be able to trust that the artist behind the music is who they say they are. That’s more essential than ever in the age of generative AI.”

Last year Spotify revealed it had removed 75m spam tracks from its platform over a 12-month period as AI tools created a flood of fake music. Spotify’s legitimate catalogue stands at 100m tracks.

Spotify will allow music creators to reveal if their identities are AI-created – and will then label them as an AI persona – but it will not rely on self-disclosure alone. The company said it would use human review and AI investigative tools to determine if artists were fake. Although the new rule technically applies to AI “identities”, Spotify says AI-generated profiles are invariably a front for AI-made tracks as well.

The company said: “Listeners have been clear in telling us that they don’t like seeing an artist profile that seems human, only to find out that the persona is AI-generated.”

Last year there was debate about the origins of the Velvet Sundown – a 70s-style US rock band – before the band’s social media channels confirmed the subterfuge. A statement described the group as an AI creation that was “somewhere in between” human and machine.

The Velvet Sundown has 117,000 monthly listeners on Spotify but its page has no clear AI labelling, although the artist profile describes the four-piece as a “synthetic music project”.

In January there was further discussion about Sienna Rose, a soul singer who entered Spotify’s viral top 50 but did not appear to be real, having never played a gig or released any videos despite releasing a prolific burst of material over a 10-week period. The Spotify profile for Rose, who has more than half a million monthly listeners, does not clarify whether she is AI or not.

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta faces expensive child safety reckoning
Gaming_Tech.text:
Hello, TechScape readers! Danielle Abril, editor of the Guardian’s Reworked series on AI and the future of work, filling in for Blake Montgomery this week. Major legal battles against Meta over child safety are playing out in courts across the US – and the tech giant is losing. Recent rulings raise big questions about social media companies’ responsibility to their youngest users. Meanwhile, more key executives have jumped ship from Google as it battles OpenAI and Anthropic in the race for AI dominance, and Meta’s smartglasses face a fearsome backlash. Let’s dig in!

Meta latest legal loss piles on the pressure as child safety concerns grow

The pressure on social media giants including Meta is mounting, as courts work through a growing pile of cases and deliver devastating, expensive rulings, one after another. Meta’s repeated losses underscore how serious the child safety crisis has become for social media companies and may force them to change how they operate to avoid further costly legal exposure.

The latest blow came last week, after a New Mexico court hit Meta with an order to pay $567m into a teen mental health fund to remediate the harm its platforms have caused children. The penalty adds to the $375m fine already on the court’s books after a jury determined in March that Meta negligently permitted damage to children’s mental health and hid what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. In a Los Angeles court, also in March, Meta was held liable for $4.2m in damages for designing platforms that addict and hurt children. The California case paved the way for hundreds of plaintiffs who have filed similar cases, which could cost Meta billions and force major changes to its products.

But New Mexico is just the latest of many headaches in store for social media companies including Meta. The company is facing 42 lawsuits filed by states across the US, plus thousands more, along with YouTube, TikTok and Snap, brought by state attorneys general, school districts and individual families.

At the center of the battle is the growing concern that social media companies harm its youngest users with addictive features that propel issues such as depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The plaintiffs’ goal is to hold companies accountable and enjoin them to change their products – everything from stricter age verification to usage limits and safety banners promoting protection features.

“This is a cautionary tale of hubris,” said Karen North, a professor at University of Southern California who studies social media. Tech companies “seemed to believe they had safe harbor, and this wasn’t their problem”.

Government-ordered remedies are a partial fix at best. For example, the New Mexico court ordered Meta to improve its age verification tools, which use artificial intelligence to analyze signals such as the ages of users’ friends and the content users post and consume. It also asked Meta to develop a prediction model that could determine if users were under the age of 13. These measures will probably flag more underage users for better protection.

But broadly, AI has a track record of misprofiling people, which will probably leave some underage users undetected. Meanwhile, inadequate age verification checks have left Australia’s ban on social media for children under 16 largely ineffective, according to recent research. Only a small percentage of those surveyed were required to provide official ID, and a significant portion said they bypassed the restrictions by using a fake account or a VPN.

Meanwhile, tech companies are already skirting some trials through private settlements. Last week, TikTok settled three lawsuits from young people over claims its app harmed their mental health. Last month, a lawsuit filed against Meta in Los Angeles was dropped after the plaintiff settled with YouTube, TikTok and Snap. In June, companies reached a settlement with a Kentucky school district that sued over platforms’ addictive designs that caused harm.

Children’s safety on social media is no longer a peripheral issue for tech giants. It’s a growing risk to companies’ bottom lines. And the outcome of a federal case against Meta, brought by attorneys general from 29 states set for trial later this month in Oakland, California, could set the tone (and price) for the thousands of cases ahead.

But, as North says, child safety is probably the tip of the iceberg. “At what point do they decide you don’t have to be a child to be harmed?” It starts with “young people and then vulnerable people and then all people”.

The backlash to Meta’s smartglasses

‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content

This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacy

Tell us: do you believe you have been filmed by Meta’s smartglasses without your consent?

Restaurants, pubs and theatres ban Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ over privacy fears

‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion

Google faces executive shake-up as it battles for AI supremacy

Google’s AI division is facing an internal leadership shuffle amid a heated external talent war, as frontier labs race to build the most capable large language models and capture the biggest market share.

News broke last week that Google’s DeepMind CEO, Demis Hassabis, is stepping down from day-to-day leadership of the famed AI unit. He will serve as the chair of DeepMind, chief scientist for Google parent Alphabet, and continue as the CEO of Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery company that spun off from Google. Meanwhile, Google’s current chief scientist, Jeff Dean, a 27-year veteran, and three colleagues are leaving to launch Discovery Loop, a startup the tech giant is backing. The news caused the company’s stock to drop 4%, and it had yet to rebound as of this newsletter.

The executive shake-up follows the exits of other key leaders, several of whom have jumped to competitors in the last year, and reports of poor morale and delayed releases – Gemini 3.5 Pro is months late and counting. With executives exiting and releases delayed, the pressure to keep pace is only mounting, especially as Google continues to trail OpenAI in the AI race.

ChatGPT is still decidedly in the lead, with 1.11 billion monthly users as of May, according to data from the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. While Gemini has steadily started to close that gap, with help from a strong Android user base and integrations across Google’s ecosystem, it lags behind with 662 million monthly users in the same month. Claude, meanwhile, has seen a spike in growth this year but trails both at 245 million monthly users, though Anthropic has captured more business customers and higher margins than OpenAI by focusing its bot on coding and technical tasks.

Still, while Google’s exits may be among the most senior and seemingly consequential, they’re part of a broader turnover happening across AI labs as competition for a minuscule pool of top talent intensifies. Which labs can hold on to those major players will shape who leads the AI race in the future.

Entertainment.title: Lucy Davis: Comedian Jasper Carrott says he is 'so proud' of daughter following her cancer diagnosis
Entertainment.text:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

In a statement on Instagram on Tuesday, Davis explained: "A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer, which has metastasised to my bones.

"Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn't bother getting it checked. So I guess I'm saying don't ignore anything - get everything checked out."

She added: "As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can... I'm not scared of whatever comes next. I'm at peace with it."

As well as The Office, Davis has appeared in Shaun of the Dead, Wonder Woman, The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip and BBC Radio 4's The Archers.

Entertainment.title: Nicholas Hoult joins Harry Potter TV show - see the cast so far
Entertainment.text:
Nicholas Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, has been cast in the hotly anticipated Harry Potter TV series.

The English actor, 36, will play Hogwarts professor Gilderoy Lockhart - who was portrayed by Sir Kenneth Branagh in the films.

The TV adaptation of JK Rowling's best-selling books will reach screens this Christmas, although Hoult will not be seen until season two.

In the stories, Lockhart was a celebrity author of books such as Magical Me before joining Hogwarts as a Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher in Harry's second year.

HBO announced the casting, external by quoting the title of Lockhart's autobiography and one of his famous lines: "Magical me indeed. Now, how many autographs would you like? Nicholas Hoult has been cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two of the new HBO original Harry Potter series."

Hoult found fame alongside Hugh Grant in the big-screen adaptation of Nick Hornby's novel About A Boy in 2002, before going on to star in teen drama Skins.

He played Hank McCoy, also known as Beast, in four X-Men movies, was Lex Luthor in the recent Superman film, was nominated for an Emmy for The Great, starred in Oscar-nominated film Nosferatu, and played the lead role in a biopic of author JRR Tolkien.

He is the latest name to join the cast for the TV version of Harry Potter, which is expected to last for a decade.

Entertainment.title: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos
Entertainment.text:
Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.

It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.

The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.

Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.

That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business.

"Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced.

"Disney owns some of the world's biggest franchises but ownership of attention is shifting towards creators," social media expert Matt Navarra told BBC News.

"Hollywood used to market at fans - now it needs to give fans the raw materials to market with it, and that is quite a profound shift."

TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.

Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.

This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.

TikTok would also benefit from the "credibility of becoming a formal distribution partner to one of Hollywood's biggest studios," Navarra said.

He added that TikTok's recommendation algorithm gives it the power to "influence which character or scene or forgotten franchise suddenly becomes very valuable again".

Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events.

"This is a deal that repositions and recovers Disney in the UGC [user-generated content] space following the content gap left by the sudden collapse of Sora," Gareth Sutcliffe from Enders Analysis said.

But he said it was not without risk.

"There is an ongoing safety debate around TikTok under European online rules," he said.

"At a minimum, Disney will need to employ significant guardrails to curate the creator content that is selected."

Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.

Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.

There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.

Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

Entertainment.title: Melanie Walters: Gavin & Stacey star completes Strictly Come Dancing 2026 line-up
Entertainment.text:
Gavin & Stacey star Melanie Walters has become the 15th and final celebrity to be announced for the line-up of Strictly Come Dancing 2026.

Walters has played mild-mannered, omelette-obsessed Gwen West in the BBC comedy since 2007, including the finale broadcast at Christmas in 2024.

In a statement, Walters said: "Performing in pantomime for the last 15 years, my Strictly 'fix' has always been watching in a dressing room rather than my front room.

"This year I am completely thrilled and happy to swap my fairy wand for sequinned dance shoes."

She added: "I just hope I don't follow Cinderella and leave one on the Ballroom stairs. I cannot wait to take part in this absolutely iconic show, it's so exciting. See you in September!"

Walters is also known for roles in Coronation Street, Beyond Paradise, Doc Martin, Being Human, Death Valley and Hollyoaks.

Her film credits include High Tide and Save the Cinema, while she has also appeared in stage productions such as Blood Brothers, Twelfth Night and Educating Rita.

All 15 celebrity contestants have now been confirmed for Strictly Come Dancing - see the full line-up below:

Team GB skeleton racer Tabby Stoecker won gold at the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, and is also a World Cup race winner, a double World Championship medallist and a European Championship medallist.

She only made her international debut in the sport five years ago.

When her participation was announced, Stoecker said she was "over the moon" to be joining this year's Strictly cast.

"I've had the wildest year of my life so far," she continued, "so to be rounding it off with a childhood dream of dancing in the Strictly ballroom is surreal and I can't wait to get stuck in!"

Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb has played Mackenzie 'Mack' Boyd in the ITV soap since 2020.

His other credits include appearing opposite Billie Piper in I Hate Suzie and in stage productions such as Legally Blonde The Musical.

In a statement, the actor joked: "I don't know who's more excited about this, me or my mother.

"I can't quite believe that I am going to be getting my dancing shoes on this September on one of my favourite shows of all time."

He added: "It's a dream come true, and I can't wait to bring my all to ballroom. Wish me luck, and any advice is very welcome - trust me I'll need it!"

Known as the Dogfather, Graeme Hall has appeared on Channel 5's Dog's Behaving (Very) Badly since the show's launch in 2017.

The presenter and dog trainer has also fronted The Dog Hospital and contributed to BBC radio programmes, ITV's This Morning, and wrote a regular column for the Times.

"I can't believe I am joining the cast of Strictly for 2026," Hall said. "I have always loved dancing, so to have the opportunity to learn from the best in the business is a dream come true.

"I have watched the show for years, so to be a part of it feels like a very exciting challenge, albeit more than a bit nerve-wracking! I can't wait to get started. Bring it on!"

Hall has also written books including The Ultimate Kid's Guide to Dogs and previously made a cameo appearance in the hit drama All Creatures Great and Small.

Other celebrities to be confirmed for Strictly this year include former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips.

The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.

His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips said this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone".

"Dancing is in my blood - but mainly at family events!" he said. "I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"

While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.

Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.

Her acting career began when she was 14 when she appeared in a short film adaptation of The Tempest, before being cast as a guest role in the BBC's Doctors.

The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.

Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"

Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Mercer was part of the winning couple on ITV dating show Love Island last year, and also works as a model and DJ, and is an ambassador for a young people's mental health charity.

"I have grown up watching the show with my family and am so excited to now be part of the cast," he said.

Mercer also showcases his Afrobeat, hip-hop and street dance moves on his social media accounts.

"Dancing is a huge passion of mine and I can't wait to learn ballroom and do the foxtrot for the first time!" he added.

Delta Goodrem is also part of this year's celebrity list, with the Australian singer and actress becoming the third celebrity to be announced for the upcoming series.

"I've been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career - from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world," Goodrem said.

"There is, however, one stage I've never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I'm absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can't wait to get started."

She rose to fame in hit Australian soap opera Neighbours and recently represented her nation in the 2026 edition of the Eurovision Song Contest.

Lacey Turner was the first contestant to be announced for this year's series, which is expected to begin in September.

She said she was "so excited to be making my way to the dance floor", adding that she was a "huge fan" of the show.

Turner, 38, is best known for her role as Stacey Slater on the BBC One soap, which she joined in 2004.

She has won a British Soap Award and National Television Award for her role, and has also starred in TV dramas including the BBC's Our Girl.

In a video posted on Instagram, Turner said she was "so excited and so terrified at the same time" to be taking part in the show.

"But I've had so many friends do Strictly, and I thought it was about time that I pluck up the courage and made my way on to the dance floor."

Dani Dyer, the media personality and daughter of actor Danny Dyer appeared in the launch episode last year, but was then injured in training and pulled out before the competition began.

That incident has not put her off trying again. "I am so excited to be back in the ballroom this September," she said.

"I just cannot wait to get my dancing shoes back on and hopefully this time around I can actually make it to week one! I'm just over the moon and cannot wait to find out who else is doing it."

The 29-year-old, who first found fame on Love Island in 2018, fractured her ankle when she "landed funny" in rehearsals with dance partner Nikita Kuzmin before the competitive episodes began last September.

She was replaced by actress Amber Davies, another former Love Island winner, who went on to reach the Strictly final.

Earlier this year, Dyer was joint winner of Channel 4's Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins, and appeared with her dad in TV show The Dyers' Caravan Park.

Entertainment.title: UK's largest Harry Potter shop comes to London's Oxford Street
Entertainment.text:
The UK's largest Harry Potter shop will open on London's Oxford Street in November, Warner Bros has announced.

The flagship store, which will span more than 21,000 sq ft (1,951 sq m) over two floors, will open within The Ribbon development at 134-140 Oxford Street on 4 November.

Warner Bros said the store was inspired by the magical shopping street Diagon Alley, and would feature a dragon towering over Gringotts bank, a full-sized Knight Bus, and The Leaky Cauldron pub where visitors can enjoy food and Butterbeer drinks.

The New West End Company called the store a "great example" of an "immersive and leisure experience" for the nation's high street.

The shop will be the second official Harry Potter retail destination in the UK after the site at King's Cross Station.

Karl Durrant, Warner Bros senior vice-president of worldwide retail, said opening the shop in London was "a truly special milestone".

"There's no better place to create a destination that celebrates the magic, creativity and storytelling that has captivated generations of fans around the world," he said.

Oxford Street is one of the world's busiest shopping areas, with around half a million visitors each day.

Entertainment.title: Welsh film lover shares home with life-sized collectibles
Entertainment.text:
Setting foot into a one-bedroom flat in an old mining village, you immediately become aware of dozens of pairs of eyes staring at you.

"My landlord used to call me Peter Pan," said 61-year-old Martin James, a former cleaner, farmer and singer who now spends much of his time buying, creating and altering his collectables.

He shares his modest-sized flat in Caerphilly county with 32 "life-sized" props, including an imposing T-800 - the Terminator played by Arnold Schwarzenegger.

He also has a 6ft, 175lb (79kg) Po, better known as Kung Fu Panda, and Pennywise, the clown from the film, It.

Overlapping action figures, posters and teddy bears also cover Martin's walls and ceilings. His collectables consist of "anything unusual", but he is mostly inspired by Hollywood.

He's far from alone and is part of a rising cohort of "kidults", who are consumers over the age of 12, who are trying to counter the "doom and gloom" of adult life, an expert said.

"They call me mad Martin and I don't know why," he laughed.

He traded his motorbike for a Terminator figure nearly 10 years ago and said his larger collectables were now increasing in value.

Martin said he was offered £10,000 for his Kung Fu Panda figure, more than the estimated value, but insists it is not about money.

"Christ, no. I'd never do it for the money. People say: 'Why collect then?' It's because I enjoy it.

"Life is too short to be boring, I don't drink, I don't smoke. If I'm going to spend any money, I'd like to show what I got out of it."

Martin's collection is a mix of rare items and props he has created or refined himself.

He says his partner has been "good as gold", helping him collect items, while his own children have grown up, allowing him to dive into his hobby.

Toy-sale tracking showed Kidults made up one-third of UK sales in 2025.

Elliot cites stories of people "quitting their jobs" to invest in items like Pokémon trading cards.

"If you do it right, and if you're incredibly clever, you can make money from it," he said.

"A lot of it can sometimes boil down to luck."

Elliot, who is a collector, said social media, influencers and celebrities like Logan Paul and Henry Cavill are helping counteract a "stigma".

"Henry Cavill looks proper manly, but he's out painting Warhammer figurines.

"He's showing off his passion, I think that's one of the best things and I think it shows that human side of people."

"I think the idea of 'childlike passions', for a psychologist, we would probably label that within a broad area of play," said Dr Julie Kirkham, leader for the MSc family and child psychology programme at the University of Chester.

Kirkham places activities such as reading fiction or creative crafts in a similar category, although these might face less stigma than an activity like Lego.

"Although these may seem childlike, they may still have important functions of allowing us to be creative, to reduce stress and take a break from complex cognitive tasks and to develop social relationships and build social bonds.

"I think it's increasingly becoming recognised that adults play as well."

Kirkham also cites play as having "therapeutic value" for exploring our emotions, experiences and memories, but in a safe space.

"But it could also just be fun, sometimes it isn't any more complicated than that."

She said the pandemic created conditions for increased interest in activities like collecting.

"Humans are a very social species, so interacting via social media offered opportunities to alleviate boredom and join communities and develop friendships."

For Martin, collecting gives him a sense of meaning: "I've had a few tragedies in my life through family and whatever else, and I think, 'enjoy life while it's here'."

Entertainment.title: Anne Hathaway pokes fun at 'fake baby bump' theories
Entertainment.text:
Anne Hathaway has poked fun at those who suggested her baby bump didn't look real after a recent film premiere, telling them she had "fake hair, real bump".

The US actress turned heads in an outfit that showed off her bare bump at the launch of her new film, The End of Oak Street, in Los Angeles on Sunday.

It sparked a flurry of comments on social media, external from people saying "Why does it look fake?" and "Oh come on. That is not real."

But others came to her defence, with one writing: "A lot of people in these comments have never seen a pregnant belly on someone who has abs." Another questioned: "Can women exist, damn," while someone else posted: "People always commenting about women is insane."

Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she is expecting her third child with husband Adam Shulman.

Celebrities are often judged on their choice of red carpet wear, but Hathaway's outfit at the premiere for The End of Oak Street has attracted particular attention.

Her bump was partially exposed in the custom Atelier Prabal Gurung crop top, which the designer described as a "sculptural high-low halter top with a cascading train". Hathaway paired the top with low-rise La Ligne jeans and red Aquazzura stilettos.

"Fake hair, real bump," the actress wrote on Instagram, external with a video of her getting ready and attending the premiere.

"Enjoy The @endofoakstreet Block Party chaos with me as my outfit literally melts in the heat!!"

As well as raising unfounded doubts about the bump, some people criticised the star's attire on social media, calling it "ridiculous", "tacky" and "bizarre".

But others praised her. Charlotte Cripps wrote in the Independent, external: "It might be an outfit that her social media critics wouldn't be seen dead in, but it's a clear message of body positivity, strength, and gender equality – and it's her unique expression of the next chapter of her life."

An op ed in Vogue stated, external: "What the rest of us need to realise is that a woman's baby bump is none of our business (can't believe this still needs saying).

"What if, instead, we celebrated the fact that a woman's body is doing something amazing, rather than telling her that she looks shameful, fake, "over the top" or "awful and a bit weird"? Now that really would be radical."

The Telegraph's Rebecca Cope said, external: "Though drawing criticism from some, the look is just the latest example of a celebrity literally letting it all hang out."

Hathaway's appearance on Sunday also led to a surge in interest in her "coconut water" nails look, external.

Entertainment.title: Amanda Knox comedy show 'sincere' but 'just not very funny'
Entertainment.text:
Amanda Knox's debut Edinburgh Fringe show has opened to mixed reactions, with critics describing it as "sincere" and "painfully unfunny".

The show, titled Cartwheel, arrived at the festival as one of this year's most talked‑about productions, attracting criticism from Meredith Kercher's sister Stephanie ahead of its first performance.

Knox, from the US, was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith in Italy in 2007.

Early reviews suggest the show, which Knox told the BBC focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women," is more of a personal, one‑woman piece than conventional stand‑up.

The Guardian awarded it four stars, external, praising its "spirit of defiance", while The Times only gave it two stars, external, calling the show "sincere" but "stilted".

The Daily Telegraph also only gave it two stars, stating Knox's performance was "so very far from great stand-up"., external

That particular opinion was echoed across several reviews, which argued that Knox is less a stand‑up comedian and more of a storyteller.

And the story she tells is extraordinary.

Knox, from Seattle, was 21 when she was arrested in Italy over the murder of her flatmate, Meredith Kercher, a student from Surrey, who was the same age.

Kercher was found dead in the house they shared while studying abroad in Perugia.

Knox's then‑boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, was also arrested.

The pair spent almost four years in prison before they were acquitted on appeal in 2011.

A retrial briefly reinstated their convictions in 2014, but Italy's top court overturned them again in 2015.

Ivory Coast-born Rudy Guede served 13 years of a 16-year sentence for Kercher's murder after his fingerprints were found at the scene.

The case's notoriety still follows Knox; since Kercher's death, Knox has written two books about her imprisonment and served as an executive producer on the biographical drama The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox.

According to The Guardian, external, she opens Cartwheel by telling the audience: "Welcome to the most controversial show at the Fringe."

The publication noted that those expecting insensitive remarks about Kercher would be proved wrong, describing Cartwheel as a "respectful" attempt to reclaim her story.

Broadway World, external gave the show three stars, emphasising that it is not "jokes about murder", but a piece about how Knox might one day explain the case to her young daughter.

Like other reviewers, it argued that the issue lies in billing the show as stand‑up comedy.

The outlet said the material is not offensive or inappropriate but was "just not very funny."

The Times, external also questioned the show's framing, saying Knox needed a director and describing Cartwheel as "more of a one‑woman show than stand‑up".

The Daily Telegraph, external echoed that a "decent director" was needed, concluding that the show is "delivered with too much act­orly poise, and no sense what­so­ever for comic tim­ing".

Taken together, the reviews paint a picture of a show shaped more by personal reflection than conventional comedy, something Knox herself acknowledges.

She told the BBC she is using comedy to explore trauma and motherhood.

"I hope people will honestly engage in my work and recognise the deep heart and sensitivity that I bring to it as I tell a very personal story," she said.

But Kercher's sister told BBC Breakfast she fears the show risks "normalising and trivialising" violence against women, and her sister, in particular.

A petition set up by a friend of Meredith Kercher gathered nearly 5,000 signatures before the show launched, arguing the show disrespects her memory.

The Fringe show has an 11-day run in the Gilded Balloon Teviot.

Its title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed Knox did cartwheels in the police station after her British roommate's death.

Entertainment.title: UK police argue Tate brothers 'a flight risk' ahead of bail hearing
Entertainment.text:
British prosecutors are urging a US court to deny a request by influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan that they be released from jail while extradition proceedings play out, ahead of a detention hearing.

They have been held in Florida since their arrest last month after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which prosecutes criminal cases in England and Wales, unveiled 38 charges against them. Both have denied wrongdoing.

The CPS has said the brothers are a "flight-risk", and would attempt to interfere with the witnesses in the case, according to court filings.

The hearing on Thursday will determine whether the brothers will remain in jail for the duration of their court proceedings.

The brothers, who are dual British-US citizens, were arrested in Miami on 19 July.

They are facing a total of 59 charges, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.

Both prosecutors and defence lawyers filed new documents on Monday in the Southern District of Florida federal court, ahead of the hearing on Thursday to decide whether they should be freed on bail.

While lawyers for the Tates acknowledged that bail in international extradition proceedings was unusual, they said the brothers had shown no reason to think they plan to evade criminal prosecution. The BBC has contacted the brothers' attorneys for comment.

Documents filed by the prosecution include a request from the British Embassy in Washington, and sent to the US Department of State, to deny bail.

Supporting documentation from the CPS was also filed highlighting alleged risks if the Tates are released on bond.

"Both Andrew and Tristan Tate have significant resources available to them, both in terms of money and in social media networks," prosecutors argued.

"All of the complainants in this case are vulnerable and in fear of Andrew and Tristan Tate because of the violence used towards them – several of the complainants describe being assaulted and threatened with weapons – and because of the resources available to Andrew and Tristan Tate, and because of their propensity to intimidate vulnerable complainants."

Prosecutors also cited social media posts made by Andrew Tate, in which he allegedly mocked prosecutors and suggested he could hide his identity to avoid arrest.

The new charges relate to four new accusers with allegations spanning from 2010-17, according to British prosecutors.

The brothers were already charged in 2025 with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the UK between 2012-15.

Police in Bedfordshire, in south-eastern England, secured European arrest warrants in 2024 for the brothers to have them returned from Romania to face the allegations.

The two moved to Romania in 2016, and were arrested on sex charges in 2022. The case there has not moved forward, and the brothers have been able to travel to the US since travel restrictions against them in Romania were lifted in early 2025.

Entertainment.title: Charlotte Church-founded school in Wenvoe operated without permission
Entertainment.text:
An outdoors school set up by singer Charlotte Church on a former pig farm has had planning permission refused for a site it had been using over environmental fears.

The Awen Project opened in 2024 without planning permission in Wenvoe, Vale of Glamorgan.

It applied for retrospective permission in October 2025, but that was refused and it has since appealed to the Welsh government's Planning and Environment Decisions Wales (PEDW).

The council raised concerns over the noise, impact on residents, and dangers to pedestrians because of insufficient parking. It also said the project failed to show how it would "conserve and enhance green infrastructure".

The Awen Project said it would not be closing.

"We have simply moved on from land that was only ever temporary - which is the model that we operate under," it said in a statement.

It added that Church had not been involved with the project for some time.

The Awen Project aims to give children an environment "where they feel championed to be themselves and follow their passions as active participants in a democratic community".

The school is free and accepts donations.

It was originally based in Cwm George and Casehill Woods, near Dinas Powys, with permission from the Woodland Trust.

But, in 2023, the charity revoked the license agreement because of "multiple breaches" of the permission granted which "posed health and safety concerns" for "visitors and wildlife".

In response, the project posted on social media that it had given its "best efforts to salvage" the partnership.

A council spokesperson said the planning application for the site in Wenvoe was refused because of "concerns regarding the sustainability" of the site's location and the "potential impact on neighbouring residents was another consideration".

There was also "insufficient supporting evidence to satisfy concerns around the potential impact of the proposal on biodiversity and the natural environment", the council said.

PEDW confirmed it had received the appeal, but said no date has been fixed for the hearing.

Entertainment.title: ‘I turned down Gandhi because I’m terrified of snakes’: the amazing movie memories of Bruce Dern
Entertainment.text:
‘Can you take another story?” asks the veteran actor Bruce Dern towards the end of our talk, as though every tale is a drink and the landlord has called last orders. He doesn’t want to keep me and knows we’re running out of time. It’s just that one memory sparks another and these tales won’t tell themselves. He says that the next one is a doozy. “It’s about Marilyn Monroe.”

Throw out all the questions and turn the clocks to the wall. One does not interview Dern so much as say hello, hit record and sit back. The man began his career acting alongside Montgomery Clift and Mary Astor and has collaborated with everyone from John Wayne to Tom Hanks, Hitchcock to Tarantino. He’s the lawless survivor of American movies, blown in from the past, and talking 19 to the dozen. “I’m 90 fucking years old,” he tells me. “So I’m not going to be around to see all this AI shit or whatever. But I don’t consider myself old. I still walk and jog every day.”

He used to run seriously and was good at it. Running, he says, taught him how to pace himself, stay focused and not lose heart when his rivals streaked ahead. “Every time I ran I used to have to come up from behind. And it was the same in showbusiness, I was always the second or third banana, never the first choice for anything. But when you’re running a marathon you learn that the first 16 miles don’t matter. It’s really only the last 10 miles that count.”

I confess that I love Dern in his lagging, dragging early years, too, when he played Jack Nicholson’s shady brother in The King of Marvin Gardens, Robert Redford’s nemesis in the 1974 version of The Great Gatsby, and the world’s last botanist in the eco-fable Silent Running. But his final straight has been a blast, a downhill dash after all those gruelling hard yards. Dern’s turn as a lost, flailing dreamer in Alexander Payne’s Nebraska won him the Cannes best actor award at the age of 77. He returned to the festival again this year as the star of a documentary tribute, Dernsie, named after his signature habit of breaking from the script. The scene in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood when Brad Pitt’s hero introduces himself as Cliff Booth, only for Dern’s befuddled old rancher to mutter, “John Wilkes Booth?” That was a Dernsie, cooked up on the spot.

Both visits to Cannes were terrific, he says. After the documentary screened, the organisers sat him on stage and the applause rolled on for six minutes. The festival boss, Thierry Frémaux, asked what that meant to him. “And I said, ‘Well, what it means is that Cannes gives a shit.’ I’ve gone through my whole life trying to find people who give a shit about Bruce Dern. And I’ve found it twice – both times in Cannes.”

Who is to say that he’s not about to find it in Scotland? Next week he’s booked at the Edinburgh film festival where his latest movie, Northbound, receives its world premiere. Dern plays incorrigible Arthur, who’s on a final lap of his own, fleeing a stuffy US nursing home for his old boyhood shack on a Canadian lake. Northbound is scratchy on the surface and sentimental underneath. It’s like Nebraska’s sweeter and sunnier cousin. “Yeah, they’re related,” Dern says, although further details elude him. “This one was a little movie that we made in Canada for about a million-six American dollars. We made it in 30 days during the Olympics. But it was two years ago now.”

I’m surprised to hear that Dern feels overlooked. He’s such a distinctive, arresting presence; the wolfish guide to America’s wonky corners, perfect at playing loners and cranks and wayward angels alike. Nicholson – his onetime rival and close friend – ranked him among the finest performers of the late-60s Easy Rider generation. If actors are cattle, Hitchcock liked to joke, “then Bruce is the golden calf”. He landed juicy roles and made money, but it was always an insecure life. It took an Oscar nomination for his role in 1978’s Coming Home to make him feel he belonged – and even then, only slightly.

Arthur in Northbound longs for his childhood home. Dern can’t relate. Where is home anyway? He was born into a wealthy, well-connected Chicago family (Adlai Stevenson was his godfather; Eleanor Roosevelt babysat) who all but disowned him when he quit college to act. He trained at the celebrated Actors Studio in New York, studying under Elia Kazan and Lee Strasberg, but was rarely given any lines and struggled to make much impression. “I got very impatient,” he says. “The other men at the Actors Studio were starting to make it: Harry Guardino, Ben Gazzara, Tony Franciosa. They were all acting and directing and going off to Hollywood. Not Brucie! I was on stage not speaking. I was still Harpo-fucking-Marx. When I finally made my Broadway debut, it was in a play called The Shadow of a Gunman. I had one scene and six lines and was on stage for 52 seconds. So you tell me, who’s going to give a shit about that?”

Now he’s on a roll; the old days bubble up. He says: “The Actors Studio had a baseball team. Our best pitcher was George C Scott. Peter Falk with one eye was our third baseman. On Memorial Day weekend we’re playing softball in the park. And Gadge – that’s what we called Kazan, Gadge – turns to me and he says: ‘What are you still doing here? Why aren’t you in California? We never said you couldn’t go.’ Well, that’s what I’d been waiting for. The next day, a Tuesday, I went to California and I never went back. Memorial Day 1960.”

Hollywood, he explains, was first his lifeline, then his base. He worked on Hitchcock’s TV show and acted in Roger Corman B-movies, before bagging his first big respectable movie in 1969’s They Shoot Horses, Don’t They? “You can’t even find that movie any more,” he tells me. “It came out, won an Oscar and then disappeared. I got a copy for my birthday. It’s probably the only one.”

I’m wondering how Kazan kept him quiet all those years. The man’s a glorious loose cannon, garrulous and digressive; two parts Ancient Mariner to one part Grandpa Simpson. His stock of stories is bottomless, although he has his favourites. Dern remembers the time he introduced Hitchcock to the director John Frankenheimer and the day Bette Davis called Joan Crawford a cunt. The Hitchcock-Frankenheimer meeting, he adds, happened the same week a stray boulder blocked the Pacific Coast Highway, which meant that you had to drive to the boulder, squeeze past on foot and then continue your journey in a second car. This in turn made him late for lunch at the Bel-Air Hotel. He says, “I don’t know if you know the Bel-Air Hotel. It’s not very big. It has, like, two storeys.”

I don’t know it, I tell him, but he has already moved on to another lunch date. This one is with Sir Richard Attenborough. The director is practically begging our hero to play the American journalist in Gandhi. Dern re-enacts the exchange; their back-and-forth dialogue. “I said, ‘Where do I have to go?’ and he said, ‘India’. I said, ‘India? The country, India?’ I said, ‘I have a confession to make. I need to run every day and I am terrified of snakes. If I run outside my hotel in the morning, will there be a guy on the steps with a basket and a snake?’ He said, ‘Probably.’” That was enough, Dern was out. “Martin Sheen ended up playing that part.”

Can I take another story? Keep them coming; the more the merrier. Dern once met Marilyn Monroe at the Actors Studio. He walked her all the way across town to her home near Sutton Place, in the east of Manhattan. At one point they passed Greta Garbo on the street and Monroe broke down crying because she thought Garbo didn’t know her.

Dern has told this story before; it’s part of his regular repertoire. All being well, he’ll be telling it another decade down the line. “I’m done,” says Arthur towards the end of Northbound, gazing out from his deck at the morning mist on the lake. By this point I suspect that the interview might be done, too. We’ve been talking for two hours and Dern’s voice has turned croaky. I thank him for his time, because he has been ridiculously generous. “You’re welcome,” he says. “Thank you for giving a shit.”

Entertainment.title: ‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit Museum
Entertainment.text:
On the main promenade along the river that runs through Ljubljana, Slovenia’s capital, tourists stop to photograph a mannequin with a bucket on its head. Dressed in a pistachio jacket and red leggings, the figure sits at a table in front of one of the houses in the historic Old Town, staring at a spilled cup of Turkish coffee, popular with Slovenes and with the other Balkan and central European citizens with whom they shared a country, until it collapsed in the early 1990s. A large sign in the background reads: “Bullshit Museum: The world is off the rails, and so are we. Yebiga!”

Yebiga, which can be loosely translated as “fuck it”, or “screw it”, is the red thread running through the museum that was launched in May and consists of five small rooms filled with mannequins wearing odd accessories, AI-generated images of laughing characters and scenes accompanying some of the jokes, framed or displayed on cardboard screens. The word encompasses the heart of Balkan humour, says the museum’s founder, Borut Kokelj, who wears a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “What part of yebiga don’t you understand?”

“Even when there’s no money, when there are no jobs, when nothing is settled, everything can be solved with humour,” he says. “And for that to work, humour must have no filter”.

Although it presents itself as the home of “Balkan” humour, the museum is primarily centred on the joke culture of the former Yugoslavia, the socialist federation that included the Balkan Peninsula countries that are now Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo.

Formed out of the wreckage of the first world war, Yugoslavia was a political project to unite southern Slav and some non-Slavic minorities under a common identity and language, then officially known as Serbo-Croatian. But the genocidal wars that accompanied Yugoslavia’s disintegration in the early 1990s demonstrated that the idea of a single Yugoslav nation lacked deep foundations. The region’s different nations have since continued to define themselves through distinct religious identities, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy and Islam, but also separate dialects and languages.

“Balkan” humour, the museum suggests, may have been the glue that held Yugoslavia’s cultural bric-a-brac in place, and it is fitting that some of the jokes on display play directly on the issue of language. “A fool is a fool in both the Cyrillic and the Latin alphabets,” reads a large poster at the entrance, using both scripts: Cyrillic, being associated with Serbs and Orthodox Christianity, and the Latin alphabet being used by other, mostly non-Orthodox nations of the dissolved state.

The armed conflicts that have shaped the region are also reflected in the exhibition, albeit indirectly. There is wordplay on the title of the controversial 1996 Serbian drama Lepa Sela Lepo Gore (literally “pretty villages burn nicely”), about a group of surrounded Serbian soldiers during the Bosnian war, here adapted into the absurdist line Lepa jela lepo goje (“Fine food fattens you up well”).

The role and power of women in society also seems to be a unifying factor. “Starleta is the first Balkan mythical being with the body of a woman and the head of a turkey”, reads an “encyclopedic” definition of a “starleta” – a woman who seeks fame and wealth through no other achievements than her (plastic surgery-assisted) beauty. “She wanted to marry a prince, but a horse had more money,” reads another, playing on the word konj (horse), which is used in many former Yugoslav nations to describe a “man”.

Kokelj, who has collected about 25,000 jokes from the region over the years, said he resisted freighting the exhibition with politically loaded humour. “If we were to exhibit all the truly ‘Balkan’ jokes, we likely wouldn’t have opened,” he admits, referring to jokes that directly address religion, ethnicity, or national symbols.

The selection also avoids jokes that mock a specific group or feature characters identified with a particular ethnic group. There are no jokes here mocking the supposed “laziness” of Montenegrins (such as this from the humour section of a local magazine: “What does a Montenegrin say before going to bed? ‘Rise, earth, so that I may lie down,’”). I find only one AI-generated “ethnic” meta-joke: it plays on the stereotype of Slovenes as a nation eager to present itself as the most “elegant” and “European”, thereby distancing itself from the rest of the region: a Slovenian man tells a joke “the Slovenian way”, using innocent euphemistic curses such as “three hundred hairy bears”, while his “Balkan” counterpart has no restraint when it comes to colourful insults.

Overall, most of the jokes address everyday issues and the absurdities of life. “Life is neither nail polish nor acetone,” reads one. “We had it better, and we still complained. Now that things are getting worse, we’re complaining again,” says another. Others focus on romantic relationships: “Love is when you look like a sack of potatoes, but she sees you as fries.” Another recurring theme is the ability to laugh at oneself: “Amateurs make mistakes, but we, the experienced ones, create catastrophes.”

There seems to be one element that holds the exhibition together to this day, though: rakija, the celebrated Balkan fruit brandy. It is served to visitors as they enter the museum and is described in one of the exhibits as “the first aid of every Balkan household”. It is also central to the definition of the infamous yebiga, which one exhibit describes as follows: “The Balkan way of saying: what are you going to do? Maximum feeling, minimum energy. It usually goes with rakija, a cigar and a song that hurts more than it should.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
BreakingNewsTab.text:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

The astronomy group suggests creating a pinhole projector, which can be done by making a hole in a piece of card. You can use the tip of a ballpoint pen to push through the centre of it.

Holding the card in one hand and a blank piece of paper in the other, face away from the Sun.

Then line the card and paper up so that an image of the Sun becomes visible on the paper.

This pinhole projector will show you the shadow being cast on the Sun replicated in miniature.

Instead of straining vegetables and pasta, you can use a colander to achieve a similar effect to that of the pinhole projector.

Eye specialist David Jones, consultant ophthalmologist at the Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust, says this is his favourite way of witnessing an eclipse.

"If you hold the colander to the Sun and you look away from the Sun, protecting your eyes, you can make not just one picture of the Sun but a hundred all at once."

Demonstrating the technique in a video on social media, he clutches a blank piece of paper behind the colander he is holding up.

It creates a kaleidoscope of images showing the Sun and the shadow cast on it during the eclipse.

An empty cereal box is ideal for making a pinhole viewer. It works similarly to the projector but should provide a clearer image.

This is because the cardboard box blocks out the surrounding sunshine and allows in only light from the direction of the eclipse.

Cut out a piece of paper that fits the bottom of the box. Open the top of the box and tape the cutout to the bottom. This will be the screen on which you see the eclipse.

Close the box and tape it shut. On one half of the top of it, cut out a small square so you can see the paper at the bottom with one eye.

On the other half, cut out another small square to match. Cut out a piece of foil that is large enough to cover this square.

Tape it down over the square and use a pin or needle to poke a hole in the middle of the foil.

Standing with your back to the Sun, use one eye to look through the open square.

Once you've lined up the hole in the foil with the Sun, you should see an image of it on the screen at the bottom. This is where you'll see the eclipse too.

You might be tempted to watch or film the eclipse using your mobile phone, either by pointing it at the Sun or taking a selfie video, but Nasa advises against this., external

"To take images when the Sun is partially eclipsed, you'll need to use a special solar filter to protect your camera, just as you'll need a pair of solar viewing glasses (also called eclipse glasses) to protect your eyes."

They also say sensors in your phone could be damaged if pointed directly at the Sun.

"This is especially true if you're using any sort of magnifying lens attachment on the phone."

When the partial eclipse becomes visible in the UK and mainland Europe on Wednesday, it will be in the evening so it will take place low in the sky.

For a better view, the Royal Astronomical Society advises you try standing somewhere more elevated than the area around you "with a clear view of the western horizon".

Whatever you do, don't look directly at the Sun.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Andy Burnham says disposable BBQ ban under consideration
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Andy Burnham has said the government is considering a ban on disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

Some retailers have already decided to voluntarily stop selling the devices, which have previously attracted warnings from fire chiefs.

It comes as Burnham chairs an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures in recent months.

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

Speaking during a visit to Stevenage, Burnham said a disposable barbecue ban was something the government was "certainly going to consider".

"I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires," he added.

Burnham did not specify whether the government was considering a restriction on the sale of disposable BBQs, or limitations on their use.

A Labour MP wrote to large retailers last week in a bid to stop them selling disposable barbecues for the rest of the summer, whilst a number of Lib Dem MPs have also backed restrictions.

The National Farmers Union has also called on local councils to issue public space protection orders to restrict their use in public areas.

Authorities including Brighton & Hove and Fylde, in Lancashire, are among councils to have used these orders to ban single-use grills in recent years.

People who defy such orders can be fined up to £100. Councils intending to issue the orders are required to consult residents beforehand, and gather evidence of an ongoing risk to quality of life in a particular area.
